top.line: Can a key leak without breaking the policy? Told, checked, never given.
top.para: A customer asked whether a key or personal data could leak without breaking a policy. Yes, if it lists only capabilities: the key is content. So policies need content rows. Three levels: told, checked, never given. A tested hook caught five of nine leaks; four experimental rules caught the rest, with no false refusals in 3,451 real commands.

in-short.line: Nine points: content rows, three levels, a hook, experimental rules, a real sweep.
in-short.para: A key can leak through an allowed action, so policies need content rows. Told is the prompt; checked is a hook; never given keeps the key out of reach. The hook caught five of nine leaks; four experimental rules, base64 refused as policy among them, caught the rest. On 3,451 real commands it refused 22, none ordinary work.

question.line: The question from one of our first customers.
question.para: Could an API key or personal data leak without breaking any Agent Behaviour Policy? For a policy that only lists capabilities, yes. If the agent may send email, the row says yes; a key pasted into the email is not a different capability. It is the same action with the wrong content.

content.line: Capabilities and content: two more kinds of row.
content.para: Reach: can the agent read the key at all? Usually it can, and the mandate needs it to use the key, not read it: excess grant. Content: disclose.secret, mandate no; disclose.personal_data, only to the person it is about. Like investment advice, a content rule is kept by a check, and a check can miss.

levels.para: Told: the prompt says never print, send or store a key; an expectation. Checked: a hook in the harness scans what goes out and comes in; deterministic, but on the agent's machine, and a setting if its account can change it. Never given: something out of reach holds the key and adds it on the way out; a boundary.

hook.line: The hook, for Claude Code, in full.
hook.para: On PreToolUse it denies a call carrying a secret or naming a secret's variable. On PostToolUse it redacts secrets before the model sees them. On Stop it blocks an answer carrying a secret or card number. It matches key formats, card numbers and the session's own secret values. Experimental rules are on by default and can be turned off.

tested.line: Nine leaks, tested with fake keys.
tested.para: Denied: a token in a command, a key sent by its variable, a key in a URL. Redacted: a result that prints the key. Blocked: an answer with a card number. Allowed: an ordinary command. Missed by the first version: a base64-encoded key, a key split and joined, and a file of secrets piped straight out.

experimental.line: Four experimental rules, and a sweep of real work.
experimental.para: Decode base64 and hex and scan them; match any ten characters of known secrets; refuse long base64 outright; refuse secrets files sent to the network. All nine cases caught, eight more tested. Over 3,451 real commands it refused 22: thirteen were the session passing its own token on the command line, seven test data, two AWS's example key.

never.para: If the key is not in the agent's environment, none of the nine cases can leak it; the agent asks a proxy or host to make the call. We do this already: the vault host holds the studio's model key, and secrets go into tools, not prompts. Personal data needs minimisation: a token instead of the card.

policy.line: What to write in the policy: three rows.
policy.para: read.secret.api_key: usually mandate no, kept out of reach by giving the key to a proxy. disclose.secret: no, checked by a hook that knows the session's own secret values. disclose.personal_data: only to its subject, minimised where possible. A leak breaks a row, and the policy shows in advance which rows are only told.

limits.para: The hook is an example, tested on seventeen cases and one session. The experimental rules may refuse other kinds of work. Regular expressions miss unknown formats, short pieces and other encodings. A hook is only as strong as its configuration. Never given needs a proxy or host. The tests used fake keys made at random.

sources.para: A conversation with one of our first customers and a voice memo of 20 October 2026; Claude Code's hooks reference; abp.sgit.ai; and earlier articles on enforcement levels, hooks, handing secrets to agents, and the Pellbridge agents.
